config.title: Lazy Loading Routes

intro.title: Lazy Loading Routes
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a Vue.js application with multiple pages that loads components only when needed, improving performance. You'll learn the core concept of lazy loading, which defers loading parts of your app until they are required. The main technologies involved are Vue Router and JavaScript's dynamic import() function. By the end, you'll understand how to split your code into smaller bundles and configure routes to load them lazily, making your app faster and more efficient.
intro.usecase: Lazy loading routes is essential for large-scale Vue applications like e-commerce platforms, admin dashboards, and content-heavy websites. When users navigate between sections like product catalogs, analytics panels, or user profiles, lazy loading ensures only the necessary code loads, keeping initial bundle sizes small. This pattern improves performance dramatically in applications with complex features like interactive data visualizations, multi-step checkout flows, or document management systems. Developers implement this to create faster, more responsive user experiences while maintaining scalable code architecture.

objectives: Configure Vue Router to implement lazy loading for route components
Construct dynamic import statements for route components using Webpack's code splitting
Apply lazy loading to specific routes in a Vue application's router configuration
Initialize route components only when their corresponding routes are accessed
Manipulate the router configuration to replace static imports with dynamic imports
Integrate lazy loading patterns into an existing Vue Router setup
Render route components asynchronously to improve initial bundle size

steps.title: Import Vue and createApp
steps.instruction: Import Vue and createApp from the 'vue' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the necessary Vue functions.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing functions from a package
import { createApp } from 'vue'
steps.expectedOutcome: The Vue and createApp functions are imported and ready to use.
successCriteria: Vue and createApp are imported from 'vue'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both Vue and createApp from 'vue'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check your import statement. You need to import both Vue and createApp from the 'vue' package.

steps.title: Import Vue Router and createRouter/createWebHistory
steps.instruction: Import createRouter and createWebHistory from 'vue-router' to enable routing functionality.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the necessary functions from the vue-router package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing functions from a library
import { createStore, createLogger } from 'vuex'
steps.expectedOutcome: The vue-router functions are imported and available for use in setting up the router.
successCriteria: createRouter and createWebHistory are imported from 'vue-router'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both createRouter and createWebHistory from 'vue-router'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports aren't quite right. You need to import createRouter and createWebHistory from the 'vue-router' package.

steps.title: Define Home component as a regular import
steps.instruction: Create a Vue component named 'Home' that returns a simple template with a heading saying 'Home Page'.
steps.hint: Define a component using a function or arrow function that returns a template string or JSX-like structure.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Home component is defined with a template that displays 'Home Page'.
successCriteria: The Home component is defined and returns a template containing 'Home Page'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Home component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the Home component, but make sure it returns a template with 'Home Page'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Home component is not defined correctly. Ensure it returns a template with 'Home Page'.

steps.title: Define About component using dynamic import syntax
steps.instruction: Create the About component using Vue's dynamic import syntax for lazy loading. Use `() => import('./About.vue')`.
steps.hint: In Vue Router, you can define a route component by directly assigning a dynamic import function to the component property.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: lazy loading a component
const LazyComponent = () => import('./LazyComponent.vue')
steps.expectedOutcome: The About component is defined as a dynamic import that will be loaded only when the route is accessed.
successCriteria: About component is defined using `() => import('./About.vue')`
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the exact syntax `() => import('./About.vue')` for the About component.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. The About component should be defined using Vue's dynamic import syntax for lazy loading.

steps.title: Define routes array with lazy loading
steps.instruction: Create a routes array that contains two route objects: one for the Home component and one for the About component using lazy loading.
steps.hint: Define a constant named 'routes' that is an array. Each route object should have a 'path' and 'component' property.
steps.expectedOutcome: A routes array is created with two route objects: one for Home (regular component) and one for About (lazy-loaded).
successCriteria: The routes array exists with two route objects, where the About route uses dynamic import syntax for its component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your routes array has both Home and About routes, and that About uses dynamic import syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The routes array is missing or incorrect. Remember to create an array with two route objects, using lazy loading for About.

steps.title: Create router instance
steps.instruction: Create a router instance using createRouter with the routes array and history mode set to createWebHistory().
steps.hint: Call createRouter with an object containing 'history' and 'routes' properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: A router instance is created and ready to be used with the Vue app.
successCriteria: The router instance is created using createRouter with the correct configuration.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using createRouter with both history and routes properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The router instance wasn't created correctly. Check the syntax and required properties.

steps.title: Create main App component
steps.instruction: Create a Vue component named App with a template that contains a <router-view> element.
steps.hint: Define a constant named App with a template property that returns the router-view element.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a root App component ready to display your routed components.
successCriteria: An App component is defined with a template containing a router-view element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your App component has a template property with a router-view element inside.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't defined correctly. Create a constant named App with a template containing router-view.

steps.title: Create Vue application instance
steps.instruction: Create the Vue application instance by calling createApp with your App component, use the router, and mount it to the '#app' element in the DOM.
steps.hint: Call createApp with your App component, then chain .use(router) and .mount('#app') to it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Vue application instance is created, configured with the router, and mounted to the DOM, ready to run.
successCriteria: createApp is called with App, .use(router) is chained, and .mount('#app') is called.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you call createApp with App, use the router, and mount to '#app'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Vue application instance isn't properly created or mounted. Check the createApp call and the .use and .mount methods.

steps.title: Add navigation links with router-link
steps.instruction: In the App component template, add two router-link elements: one for the Home route with text 'Home' and one for the About route with text 'About'.
steps.hint: Use the <router-link> component with the 'to' attribute set to the route path. Place them before the <router-view>.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component template will include navigation links for Home and About routes.
successCriteria: The App component template contains two <router-link> elements with correct 'to' attributes and text content.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have both router-link elements with the correct 'to' attributes and text.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've added two <router-link> elements with 'to' attributes pointing to '/' and '/about'.

steps.title: Verify lazy loading in browser dev tools
steps.instruction: Open your browser's developer tools, navigate to the Network tab, and click the 'About' link to observe the About component being loaded as a separate network request.
steps.hint: Look for a new network request to 'About.vue' or similar when you click the 'About' link, confirming the component is lazily loaded.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll see the About component loaded as a separate network request only when navigating to the '/about' route, confirming lazy loading is working.
successCriteria: Network tab shows a separate request for About.vue when clicking the 'About' link, not on initial page load.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're looking in the Network tab and clicking the 'About' link to trigger the lazy load.
steps.feedbackWrong: Open browser dev tools, go to Network tab, then click the 'About' link to see the separate network request.
